query: For CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys (X = Si, Mn, or Al) in a single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain whether a stable, coherent protective oxide layer forms and persists during exposure above 900 °C in an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere, rather than developing unstable surface oxides that crack or spall? Specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison against a defined baseline, the predicted differences, the applicable exposure and material-state boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a falsifying observation.

generation.hypothesis: In CrFeCoNiX high‐entropy alloys, the identity of the X element governs the formation and persistence of a protective oxide layer at temperatures above 900 °C: Si, when present, promotes the selective formation of a continuous, viscous, and adherent silica‐rich (SiO2) scale that suppresses further oxidation and resists spallation, whereas Mn or Al favor the formation of less coherent oxides that tend to crack or spall under thermal stress.
generation.material_initial_state: CrFeCoNiX alloy in a single-phase or multiphase metallic solid-solution state, with X being either Si, Mn, or Al uniformly distributed in the matrix.
generation.intervention: Exposure to an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere at temperatures above 900 °C.
generation.conditions: High-temperature (>900 °C) exposure in air or similar oxidative/corrosive environments; experiments performed under identical processing and microstructural conditions to control for phase uniformity.
generation.structural_mediator: The nature and continuity of the oxide scale forming at the alloy surface—specifically, a viscous, glassy SiO2 layer versus less adherent, brittle Mn- or Al-based oxides.
generation.mechanism: Selective oxidation kinetics controlled by the X element: Si, with its inherent ability to form low-diffusivity, high-viscosity SiO2, creates a coherent, protective barrier that limits oxygen ingress and thermal stresses, whereas Mn or Al oxidize to form scales that are more prone to volume changes and cracking due to faster diffusion rates and poorer adhesion.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under identical high-temperature oxidative conditions, the Si-containing alloy will develop and maintain a stable, coherent protective oxide layer that minimizes further oxidation and spallation, while the Mn- or Al-containing alloys will form discontinuous, cracked, or spalled oxide scales that degrade protection.
generation.baseline: A controlled comparison where the alloy with X = Si serves as the baseline exhibiting the stable oxide behavior, against which alloys with X = Mn or Al (having otherwise similar processing and microstructure) are compared.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys in their (mostly) single-phase solid solution state, under high-temperature exposure (>900 °C) in oxidative or corrosive atmospheres. It may not hold if substantial secondary phase segregation or processing-induced defects alter the oxidation kinetics.
generation.uncertainty: The precise oxide thickness, crack density, and quantitative protective properties may vary with minor processing differences and exact microstructure; additional factors such as grain size or trace impurities might also influence the oxidation behavior.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate a series of CrFeCoNiX alloys with X = Si, Mn, and Al using identical melting and processing routes to ensure similar microstructures. Expose samples to an oxidative atmosphere at 950 °C for a fixed duration. After exposure, perform controlled thermal cycling to simulate service conditions and assess oxide layer stability.
measurements: Surface and cross-sectional microscopy (e.g., SEM/TEM) to evaluate oxide layer continuity and crack/spall formation
XRD and EDS mapping to determine the oxide phase composition and the extent of elemental segregation
Adhesion tests (e.g., microindentation or scratch test) to quantify oxide–substrate adhesion strength
Thickness measurements of oxide scales via profilometry or TEM
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Si-containing alloy does not exhibit a significantly more continuous, adherent, and less cracked oxide layer compared to the Mn- or Al-containing alloys—or if all variants show similar oxide stability—the hypothesis would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
Oxidation Behavior of FeNiCoCrMo0.5Al1.3 High-Entropy Alloy Powder

Abstract: One of the most promising applications of FeNiCoCrMoAl-based high-entropy alloy is the fabrication of protective coatings. In this work, gas-atomized powder of FeNiCoCrMo0.5Al1.3 composition was deposited via high-velocity oxygen fuel spraying. It was shown that in-flight oxidation of the powder influences the coating’s phase composition and properties. Powder oxidation and phase transformations were studied under HVOF deposition, and during continuous heating and prolonged isothermal annealing at 800 °C. Optical and scanning electron microscopy observation, energy dispersive X-ray analysis, X-ray diffraction analysis, thermogravimetric analysis, differential thermal analysis, and microhardness tests were used for study. In a gas-atomized state, the powder consisted of BCC supersaturated solid solution. The high rate of heating and cooling and high oxygen concentration during spraying led to oxidation development prior to decomposition of the supersaturated solid solution.
